listening.title: Joining a neighbourhood walking group
listening.script:
Volunteer: Hello, Green Routes walking group. You’re speaking to Max.
Caller: Hello. I’d like to join one of your weekend walks. I saw a leaflet at the health centre, but it listed several groups and I wasn’t sure which one was suitable. I walk to work, though I haven’t done anything long in the countryside recently.
Volunteer: Our introductory route would be a sensible start. It’s mostly level and has places to stop. Could I take your name first? We keep a list so that the leader knows whom to expect, but we don’t ask for medical details on the telephone.
Caller: It’s Joel Ashby. That’s A-S-H-B-Y. My cousin has the same surname with an extra letter, so I usually spell it. Is there an annual membership payment?
Volunteer: There is for the longer programme, but your first walk costs nothing. You can decide about joining afterwards. The next introductory one is on Sunday. We used to run it on Saturday, but the leader now works then.
Caller: Sunday is better for me anyway. Where do you meet? The leaflet mentioned the station.
Volunteer: That was the starting point while the footbridge was being repaired. We’re back at the museum now, beside its main doors. It’s easy to find from the bus stop, and there’s shelter if people arrive early.
Caller: And how early is early? I prefer not to rush off a bus straight into a long walk.
Volunteer: We gather at nine fifteen and leave at nine thirty. Put 9:15 in your diary, because the leader gives a short briefing before departure. If you’re delayed, call the number on the confirmation rather than trying to catch up alone.
Caller: How far will we go? I can manage four kilometres comfortably, but eight might be a bit much the first time.
Volunteer: This one is six kilometres. There’s a shorter return option if someone needs it, although most people complete the full route. We don’t use the speed of the fastest person to set the pace. The leader stays aware of the group and a second volunteer walks at the back.
---
Caller: I own ordinary trainers. Would I need to buy boots before coming?
Volunteer: Not for this route if it’s dry. Trainers with a good grip are fine. Please bring a waterproof, though. A forecast can change, and the riverside section has nowhere to shelter. A large umbrella is awkward on the narrow path, so a jacket is more useful.
Caller: Should I bring lunch as well?
Volunteer: A snack and some water. We finish near a café, but buying anything there is entirely optional. Carry a bottle rather than depending on places along the way, since the public fountain is currently out of use.
Caller: I sometimes use a walking pole. Is the path wide enough for that?
Volunteer: Yes. There’s one section with a stile, but we use a nearby gate instead. We don’t go up the steps shown on an older route map. If you have any concerns about the gate width or surface, the leader can discuss them before the day.
Caller: That sounds reassuring. Can people bring dogs? My neighbour might come, and hers is very calm.
Volunteer: Dogs aren’t permitted on this particular walk because we cross a field containing livestock. Some of our other routes welcome them. It isn’t a general judgement about well-behaved dogs; it’s an agreement with the farmer for this route.
Caller: Fair enough. What happens if there’s severe weather? Would you call everyone?
Volunteer: We send a text by eight that morning if we cancel. For ordinary rain the walk usually goes ahead, but strong wind near the trees is different. Please reply to acknowledge a cancellation so we know you won’t travel unnecessarily. I’ll send a confirmation now with the route description and the leader’s contact number.

listening.title: An orientation talk at a community arts centre
listening.script:
Director: Welcome to everyone starting a course at the Foundry Arts Centre. The building was once a small factory, but its new name isn’t an invitation to operate industrial equipment. We run practical arts courses for adults, and some family sessions during school holidays. Today I’ll describe five activities you may want to try and then explain how the centre works. You don’t have to decide everything this morning. The aim is to help you understand which course fits the time and experience you actually have.
First, bookbinding. This starts next week and lasts four Tuesday evenings. Materials are provided, but we require a reservation because the tutor prepares a separate pack for each person. Turning up on the first evening and hoping to find an empty chair won’t work, even if someone is absent. We can often offer a place on the next course instead.
The lunchtime sketch group is quite different. There is no advance booking and no expectation that you already draw well. Its special arrangement is that it’s held outside the centre, in the covered market across the road. The group meets under the market clock. This gives people moving subjects to draw, and traders have agreed that participants may sit along the wall without blocking customers.
For textile printing, you should bring something of your own to print on. A plain cotton bag is ideal; a smooth T-shirt is another possibility. We provide inks and tools, but not the fabric item itself. Please avoid a favourite expensive garment for your first experiment. The tutor will explain why different surfaces absorb colour differently.
Our percussion session has been moved to an earlier time. People used to arrive at seven on Wednesdays; it now begins at six, because the neighbouring room is needed for a quiet class later in the evening. That’s a permanent change for this term, not just for the first week.
Finally, the clay modelling course allows children to attend, provided an adult takes the course with them. It isn’t a supervised drop-off club. Both people make something and can help each other. If you were hoping to work completely on your own, choose the adults-only session on the other day.
---
Now for some general information. Membership fees cover the shared studio space and basic maintenance. They don’t cover every course material. We used to charge one inclusive fee, but someone taking only sketching was helping pay for expensive clay. Separating the costs makes the arrangement more transparent, even though the price list is slightly longer.
Our noticeboard displays examples of work, but you don’t have to agree to public display. Some people enjoy sharing a first attempt; others want to practise privately. Ask the tutor to mark your work as not for display. That decision will have no effect on your access to future courses or the amount of help you receive.
Equipment may stay in the studio between sessions, but unfinished pieces must have a name and date. Unlabelled work is difficult to store responsibly because staff can’t tell whether it has been abandoned. We won’t throw things away immediately. After a published storage period, we’ll contact the maker where possible and clear space for current classes.
The café next door offers a small discount to course members on weekday afternoons. It is independent of the centre, so please raise food orders with café staff rather than a tutor. We mention it because many students like to continue talking after class, not because a café purchase is part of membership.
Please tell us if you need adjustments to take part. The best time is when you book, because some arrangements require planning. However, if you discover a difficulty during a session, speak to the tutor then. We don’t expect you to predict every problem in advance. The office can discuss an alternative rather than simply telling you to wait until the next term.

listening.title: Reviewing an interview project
listening.script:
Tutor: Come in, Amira and Ben. I’ve read your proposal about independent shopkeepers. You’ve found an interesting question about how businesses adapt when a street changes, but I think we need to look closely at recruitment.
Amira: We’ve made a list from the traders' association website. It seemed better than walking along the street and approaching whoever wasn’t busy.
Tutor: It’s organised, certainly. But remember that the association includes only members. Shops that closed recently won’t appear, and new businesses may not have joined. If you use it alone, you’ll hear from a particular surviving group.
Ben: We could add names from older street directories and contact the former owners where details are public. We can’t guarantee they’ll agree, but at least the recruitment frame wouldn’t automatically exclude them.
Amira: Should we ask the association chair to conduct the introductions? People know her, so perhaps they’d speak more freely.
Tutor: She can circulate an invitation. I wouldn’t have her sitting in the interviews. A trader might hesitate to criticise a scheme the association supported. Make clear that the project isn’t a performance review and that individual statements won’t be sent to her.
Ben: Our draft starts with, 'How has the new pedestrian area improved your business?' I can see now that assumes an improvement.
Amira: We should ask what changed, if anything, and then invite positive and negative examples. Otherwise we’d be providing the conclusion in the question.
Tutor: Good. You’ll also need to distinguish memory from records. Someone may recall fewer customers during construction, but sales figures could follow a different pattern. Ask whether records are available without making their participation depend on handing over private accounts.
Ben: We planned an audio recording rather than trying to write everything while they speak. We’d ask permission first and offer a note-only interview if they prefer.
Tutor: That’s sensible. Explain where the file will be kept and when it will be deleted. Permission to talk to you is not permission to put a voice recording on a public website.
---
Amira: We made a checklist of remaining tasks. For the recruitment invitation, we need approval from you before sending it. We’ve drafted it but haven’t contacted anyone yet.
Tutor: Send it after this meeting. The interview schedule is different: its wording needs a trial. Ask somebody outside the final sample to respond, so you can see whether the order makes sense and how long it takes.
Ben: The street map is finished. We’ve marked present businesses and former addresses from the directories, and checked that none of the symbols hides the street names.
Tutor: Fine, treat that as completed for now. Don’t spend another day improving its colours at the expense of preparation.
Amira: We also had a question asking each trader for their exact annual income. It doesn’t answer our revised question and might put people off, so we intend to remove it.
Tutor: I agree. You can ask how they describe changes without collecting an unnecessary financial profile. Remember that an interview isn’t improved merely by making it longer.
Ben: Our coding categories are still provisional. We thought we’d wait until after the first interviews before deciding the final set. We have broad interests, but people may describe problems we haven’t anticipated.
Tutor: Yes, retain that flexibility. Keep a record of changes to the categories, though. You shouldn’t quietly redefine them every time you encounter an inconvenient example.
Amira: Would it be useful to compare two of us coding the same short extract?
Tutor: Very useful, as a way to discuss interpretation rather than produce a ceremonial agreement figure. If you disagree, ask whether the categories are unclear or the account genuinely supports more than one reading. The explanation of that decision may be more valuable than an artificially neat table.

listening.title: The changing idea of a standard measure
listening.script:
Lecturer: Think about buying a length of cloth from someone you have never met. The transaction requires more than agreement about price. You need a shared understanding of length. Today I’ll discuss standard measures as a social arrangement as well as a technical achievement. A measure is useful when different people can reproduce it closely enough for the task. That does not mean every task needs the same precision. Selling cloth and testing an optical instrument place different demands on the system, even though both involve statements about distance.
Early local arrangements often used a physical reference kept in a public place. Traders could compare their own rods with it. The object represented authority as well as length: somebody had to decide who could inspect it and what happened if a trader’s measure differed. Copies made trading easier, but each copy introduced the possibility of error. Wear, damage and the method of comparison could change the result. The practical problem was not solved simply by declaring that one reference existed. People needed a dependable chain connecting everyday measures to it.
Expansion of trade increased the value of compatibility. Two towns could each have internally consistent measures and still face confusion when goods moved between them. Converting between systems required tables or specialist knowledge, and a familiar unit name did not always mean a familiar quantity. Shared measures could reduce that work, though adopting them imposed costs of its own. Tools had to be changed, labels rewritten and users trained. Resistance was not necessarily ignorance. A new system could offer broad benefits while asking particular workers to bear immediate expense.
Calibration is the process of comparing an instrument with a suitable reference and establishing how its readings relate to that reference. It does not mean making every instrument perfect. A useful calibration record can describe an error and the uncertainty around it. For example, a workshop may apply a correction when using an instrument rather than replacing it immediately. The important point is that the reading should not be treated as exact merely because it appears as a number. Extra digits on a display can create an appearance of knowledge that the measurement process does not support.
Temperature provides a straightforward example of environmental influence. A material may expand or contract as conditions change, so a physical reference needs specified conditions of use. Handling, storage and comparison procedures become part of the definition in practice. Modern systems aim for references that can be reproduced in different laboratories, but reproducibility still requires procedures and trained judgement. It is misleading to contrast an entirely social past with an entirely objective present. Social cooperation makes technical comparison possible in both cases, even when the scientific basis becomes more stable.
Documentation allows the chain of comparison to be checked. A certificate should identify the instrument, the reference, the conditions and the relevant date. Without traceability, a precise-looking result may be difficult to connect to anything beyond the local device. This matters when several organisations contribute to one product. A component made in one workshop must fit another made elsewhere, and differences may not become visible until assembly. Shared measurement practice allows organisations to investigate a mismatch rather than merely argue about whose number looks more convincing.
Finally, standards must be maintained as living arrangements. A reference that nobody can access, or a procedure that ordinary laboratories cannot follow, may fail despite theoretical elegance. Institutions provide training, comparisons and opportunities to question results. The achievement is not the elimination of every uncertainty. It is the creation of a reliable way to describe and reduce uncertainty for a particular purpose. Standard measures make cooperation possible because they organise disagreement: when numbers differ, there is a route back through evidence, conditions and references instead of only a contest of authority.

reading.title: A city learns to deliver differently

paragraphs.A: Every morning, delivery vans entered the narrow streets around Halden Market carrying goods for small independent shops. Many left almost empty after visiting a single customer. Shopkeepers complained about congestion but resisted a proposal to keep vehicles outside the centre: they depended on reliable deliveries and feared another administrative burden. The eventual experiment began with a practical offer rather than a restriction. A warehouse near the ring road would receive consignments from different suppliers, combine them, and complete the final journey with electric cargo cycles. Participation was voluntary during the first six months.
paragraphs.B: The project manager, Rosa Vale, expected the strongest interest to come from shops selling light, expensive products. In fact, a bakery became one of the earliest regular users. Its flour sacks were too heavy for an ordinary bicycle, but the project's three-wheeled cycles had enclosed load compartments and were designed for commercial loads. The bakery valued predictable arrival times more than the environmental message. Its owner could schedule preparation without leaving a worker watching the street. This response changed the project's publicity, which began emphasising reliability alongside reduced traffic rather than assuming that every business shared the same motivation.
paragraphs.C: Not every product was suitable. A florist found that delicate arrangements moved during sharp turns unless special supports were fitted. A furniture shop continued receiving large tables directly by lorry, though smaller fittings travelled through the warehouse. These exceptions were recorded instead of being treated as embarrassing failures. The manager wanted a service that removed appropriate journeys, not a claim that one vehicle could replace every other vehicle. Staff kept dimensions and handling instructions with each booking so that an unsuitable consignment could be redirected before it reached the loading bay and delayed other customers.
paragraphs.D: The warehouse initially asked shops to make orders by midday for next-morning delivery. This suited some businesses but not restaurants that adjusted purchases after the evening service. A later collection from suppliers was introduced on three nights each week. It increased staffing costs, yet also attracted enough regular users to make better use of the morning cycles. The project did not publish a standard saving per delivery, because costs depended on distance, load and how consistently a shop used the service. Monthly statements instead separated the handling charge from the charge for the final journey.
paragraphs.E: Routes were planned with local knowledge as well as software. The shortest line on a map could involve steep cobbles, steps or a market entrance closed during trading hours. Riders marked these problems on a shared map, and the route planner updated permitted approaches. The city also installed secure loading stands near several shops. Without these, a rider might have to leave a loaded cycle while carrying goods around a corner. Reducing that risk mattered for insurance and for the willingness of riders to accept the work, not simply for the speed of individual deliveries.
paragraphs.F: Evaluating the trial proved more difficult than counting cycles leaving the warehouse. Some suppliers had previously combined deliveries to several shops on a single van trip. Replacing one shop's parcel did not necessarily remove that trip. The evaluation therefore asked suppliers about routes, not just the number of consignments transferred. It also counted travel between suppliers and the warehouse. These additional movements reduced the estimated traffic benefit but made the comparison more credible. The researchers warned that figures from the first months reflected volunteers who were particularly willing to cooperate and might not represent later customers.
paragraphs.G: Residents noticed another change that was absent from the original spreadsheet. With fewer vehicles blocking shop fronts at breakfast time, the pavement became easier to use, especially for people pushing prams. However, some residents objected when cycles were parked across pedestrian routes. The council introduced marked stopping areas and required riders to dismount in the busiest pedestrian section. The scheme's environmental intention did not exempt it from ordinary questions about public space. Shopkeepers were asked to report problems as well as praise so that the trial would not be evaluated entirely through its organisers' expectations.
paragraphs.H: When the six months ended, the service continued with fewer subsidies but a narrower delivery area. Serving distant customers had consumed disproportionate time, while regular central routes were becoming viable. The revised boundaries disappointed some businesses, yet avoided promising universal coverage that the service could not sustain. Halden's experience suggests that delivery reform is partly a problem of coordination: suppliers, shops, riders and street managers must change compatible parts of their routines. A different vehicle helps, but it succeeds within an arrangement of schedules, handling practices and realistic limits rather than through technology alone.

paragraphs.A: Night-time lighting is often discussed in terms of brightness, but brightness alone describes neither the experience of a street nor its effect on the surrounding environment. A lamp may illuminate a doorway while sending light into bedroom windows or beyond a riverbank. Another may leave a pavement unevenly lit despite producing more total light. In a fictional research programme, the town of Calder investigated where its lighting went and how different people used it. The starting point was not a commitment to darkness. It was recognition that good lighting requires a purpose and a location.
paragraphs.B: Lighting engineer Arun Mehta began by mapping lamps and measuring illumination on the pavement. His map showed large differences between adjacent streets that had been upgraded in different decades. Replacing every old lamp immediately would have exhausted the budget without establishing which changes mattered. Mehta proposed a staged trial in which matched streets received new fittings at different times. Measurements continued on streets awaiting replacement. This arrangement helped separate the effects of the trial from changes affecting the whole town, such as seasonal shifts in commuting and the amount of natural light during evening journeys.
paragraphs.C: Ecologist Beth Rowan examined a footbridge crossing a small stream. Lamps on its railings directed light onto the water as well as the walking surface. She recommended shields that limited the sideways beam. Her team recorded insect activity before and after installation, while also recording wind and temperature. An increase near one lamp could represent attraction to the light rather than growth in the local insect population. Rowan therefore resisted the simple claim that seeing more insects always indicated a healthier site. The pattern of movement mattered, including whether activity was being concentrated away from neighbouring dark areas.
paragraphs.D: For social researcher Cora Blake, a technically uniform pavement was not automatically a comfortable route. She accompanied volunteers on evening walks and asked where they hesitated. Several pointed to the transition from a very bright shopping entrance to a much dimmer side street. Their concern involved sudden contrast rather than the side street's measured brightness alone. Blake also interviewed people who avoided evening walking entirely. Surveying only pedestrians already on the route would have omitted them and exaggerated satisfaction. Her sample was designed to include absence as a form of relevant behaviour, not merely as missing data.
paragraphs.E: Business representative Dan Wu initially feared that reduced lighting would discourage late customers. He agreed to a trial after the council separated decorative lighting from the lights used for entrances and steps. Shop signs could switch off after closing while essential access lighting remained. Wu asked businesses to log actual closing times, since a fixed schedule based on official hours would not cover seasonal events. Some shops closed early on quiet evenings; others held occasional late workshops. A flexible arrangement required more communication than a single town-wide switch, but avoided treating every commercial frontage as if it had identical needs.
paragraphs.F: The trial's energy figures were easier to calculate than its social outcomes. Meter readings showed the electricity used by each circuit, but a fall in reported complaints did not prove that everyone preferred the new lighting. Residents might not know where to report concerns or might assume the decision was final. Blake distributed paper feedback cards as well as an online form and returned to several households that had not replied. These efforts did not create a perfectly representative sample. They did reveal problems that would have disappeared from an evaluation relying exclusively on the most convenient reporting channel.
paragraphs.G: There were disagreements about which results should determine the next investment. Mehta favoured repairing the least efficient circuits, while Rowan wanted attention to a sensitive riverside section that used relatively little electricity. Both positions could be supported by evidence because they pursued different objectives. The council published the trade-off rather than combining every measure into an unexplained score. Its final programme reserved part of the budget for ecological locations and part for general replacement. No claim was made that the chosen division was the only scientific answer; it was a public decision informed by several kinds of expertise.
paragraphs.H: Calder's imagined programme demonstrates why the phrase better lighting cannot be reduced to either more light or less light. A fitting can use less energy and still direct light badly. A well-lit route can still be difficult to enter, and an apparently popular policy can overlook people least likely to comment. The value of the trial lay in making these distinctions observable. It provided a method for revising decisions, not a final design suitable for every street. The town treated lighting as an ongoing service to different users rather than as a product whose quality ended with installation.

reading.title: When a copy is an achievement

paragraphs.A: Originality has an attractive place in accounts of creativity. We celebrate the first version of an idea and often treat later copies as evidence of limited imagination. Yet much skilled activity depends on reproducing something well enough to discover what its description leaves unsaid. A musician learns another player's phrase; a craftsperson reconstructs an old joint; a researcher repeats a procedure. These activities are not equivalent in every respect, but they expose a weakness in the assumption that copying and understanding are opposites. Reproduction can be a demanding way of asking how an achievement became possible.
paragraphs.B: There are, of course, copies whose purpose is deception. An imitation sold as an original painting misrepresents its history, whatever the technical skill involved. Condemning that deception does not establish that all imitation lacks educational value. The relevant question is what claim is made for the copy and what work it enables. A clearly labelled reconstruction invites comparison. A counterfeit prevents it by concealing the distinction on which a fair judgement depends. The difference concerns honesty about provenance as well as visual resemblance, and a discussion that ignores provenance confuses two quite separate kinds of value.
paragraphs.C: In a fictional design class, students are asked to rebuild a simple folding stool from photographs and measurements. Many initially think the task will require little interpretation because the object is so familiar. Difficulties appear when they decide how much clearance the moving parts need and how to assemble joints without trapping the frame. These matters are not obvious in a completed photograph. When students later design their own stools, they can explain why a particular attractive shape will not fold safely. Their copied object has become evidence of decisions, not merely a substitute for the photographed original.
paragraphs.D: This does not imply that accurate reproduction automatically creates transferable expertise. A student can follow a memorised sequence while misunderstanding its purpose. Teachers therefore need to vary the conditions: a different material, an altered scale or a constraint on available tools. If the learner adapts successfully and can justify the adaptation, there is stronger evidence of understanding. The variation is useful precisely because it interrupts effortless repetition. Copying becomes educational when it makes features available for inspection and revision, rather than when it rewards the preservation of an unexamined routine.
paragraphs.E: The same distinction helps explain why a detailed written recipe may fail to reproduce a skilled performance. Experts often omit actions that have become automatic: testing a surface with a fingertip, listening for a change in a tool, or waiting until a material feels right. A novice needs these cues named or demonstrated. Observing a performance and attempting a copy can make such omissions visible to both learner and expert. The expert may then improve the instructions. Knowledge is not simply transferred from a complete document into an empty learner; the act of teaching can reveal that the document was incomplete.
paragraphs.F: Digital tools introduce a different situation. A file can be duplicated with great accuracy without the person pressing the button learning anything about its construction. This is not a criticism of duplication, which is often exactly what the task requires. It is a reminder that similarity in the result does not prove similarity in the process. Rebuilding a model and downloading it can produce indistinguishable outputs while providing very different learning opportunities. Assessments that inspect only the final object therefore need caution if their stated purpose is to evaluate the maker's reasoning, not merely the object's usefulness.
paragraphs.G: Nor should reconstruction erase the social setting of an earlier work. Reproducing a historic tool with modern machinery can demonstrate its geometry while revealing little about the time, labour or organisation once required to make it. A responsible account states which conditions were replicated and which were changed. Such limits do not render the copy worthless. They identify the questions it can answer. An experiment need not recreate an entire past world to be informative, but it must not use success under one set of conditions as proof that the same success occurred under another.
paragraphs.H: The strongest defence of copying is therefore neither that everything is imitation nor that originality is a myth. It is that different activities deserve evaluation against their actual purposes. A copy may preserve access, reveal a hidden technique, test a description or prepare someone to innovate. It may also deceive or merely repeat. We should ask which of these things it does before deciding that its secondary status settles its worth. Creativity includes the ability to depart from a model, but that departure often becomes meaningful only after someone has understood what the model demands.

writing.prompt: The charts compare how households in the fictional town of Larton allocated their average monthly expenditure in 2005 and 2025. The totals are given below each chart. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
writing.visual:
![Household spending shares](writing-1.svg)

| Category | 2005 share | 2025 share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Housing | 25% | 35% |
| Food | 30% | 20% |
| Transport | 20% | 15% |
| Leisure | 15% | 20% |
| Other | 10% | 10% |

Average total monthly expenditure: 2005, 1,200 currency units; 2025, 2,000 currency units. Figures are nominal; no inflation adjustment is supplied.
writing.guidance: Housing replaces food as the largest share. Housing and leisure shares rise; food and transport fall; other is unchanged as a share. Shares are not amounts: food rises from 360 to 400 units despite falling from 30% to 20%; transport rises from 240 to 300. Other rises from 120 to 200. Do not infer changes in purchasing power from nominal figures.

writing.prompt: In many cities, workers travel long distances between home and work. What problems can this cause for individuals and communities? What measures could reduce these problems? Give reasons and relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
writing.guidance: Develop both problems and measures. Individual costs can include time, fatigue and expense; community effects might include congestion or uneven demand. Match proposals to problems and consider practical limits. A response about the benefits of travel alone does not address the task.
